prompt: A school play sold $10^3$ tickets at $\$8$ each. Putting on the play cost the school $\$1{,}500$. How many dollars does the school have left after paying the costs?
hint: Turn the power of ten into a regular number first. Then find the money the tickets brought in before taking away the costs.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try smaller numbers first: $10^1 = 10$ tickets at $\$8$ is $\$80$, and if costs were $\$30$ you would have $80 - 30 = \$50$ left. Turn the power of ten into a plain number, multiply, then subtract — exactly the same three moves.
Turn the power of ten into a regular number first. Then find the money the tickets brought in before taking away the costs.
$10^3 = 1{,}000$ tickets, so the money taken in is $1{,}000 \times 8$ dollars. After that, subtract the $1{,}500$ dollars in costs.

explanation: First find the number of tickets by writing the power as a regular number: $10^3 = 1{,}000$.
Each ticket brings in eight dollars, so the money taken in is $1{,}000 \times 8 = 8{,}000$ dollars.
The costs must be paid out of that money, so subtract: $8{,}000 - 1{,}500 = 6{,}500$ dollars.
The school has $6{,}500$ dollars left after paying the costs.

alternativeExplanations.title: Subtract in friendly pieces
steps: The money from ticket sales is $10^3 \times 8 = 1{,}000 \times 8 = 8{,}000$ dollars.
Split the cost of $1{,}500$ into $1{,}000$ and $500$, then take off the thousand first: $8{,}000 - 1{,}000 = 7{,}000$.
Take off the last $500$ to finish: $7{,}000 - 500 = 6{,}500$ dollars left.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: A very common wrong answer is $8{,}000$, the money taken in, with the costs never subtracted.
Another mistake is reading $10^3$ as $10 \times 3 = 30$, which gives only $30 \times 8 = 240$ dollars of sales.
Remember that $10^3$ means $10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1{,}000$, and the word **left** calls for a subtraction: $8{,}000 - 1{,}500 = 6{,}500$.
